title: Did We Find Them All?
coreInsight: A difficult universe can be partitioned into cases that are exhaustive, non-overlapping, and easier to count.
targetLearnerRealization: Good casework partitions every possibility exactly once into categories that are easier to count.
learningObjectives: Recognize why sorting a partial list does not prove completeness.
Choose a useful feature to split possibilities into smaller groups.
Finish every group, check that nothing is missing or repeated, and combine the counts.

continuity.openingCallback: Remember how a careful list helped you keep track? Now we will ask how to know when that list is truly finished.
closingSeeds: A clean split can become cumbersome when the most obvious groups overlap.

misconceptionTargets.misconception: A few natural cases are automatically exhaustive.
Cases are useful even when each is as difficult as the original problem.
The best case split need not reflect the problem's actual constraint.

beats.purpose: Let an informal list feel plausible before the learner has a way to prove it complete.
beats.expectedRealization: Finding four working paths is not yet proof that there are only four.
beats.transitionIn: Remember how a careful list helped you keep track? Try this one in whatever order makes sense to you.
beats.transitionOut: We found four paths. But finding four is not the same as proving the list is finished.
beats.whyNow: A four-outcome movement puzzle makes informal listing easy while leaving a genuine completeness question.
beats.entryBridge: List the moves you find. Do not worry about sorting them yet.
beats.exitBridge: These four paths work. The next question is whether another path could still be hiding.
learnerPrompts: Write each sequence before entering your total.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Keep your attempt. Now compare it with the paths below.

visual.ariaLabel: Four animated paths moving from position zero to position three

steps.title: Check the paths we found
steps.body: Each one starts at 0, ends at 3, and uses only moves of size 1, 2, or 3.

resolution.takeaway: These four paths work. We still need to ask: did we get every possibility?

beats.purpose: Make the gap between finding examples and proving completeness explicit through a guided choice.
beats.expectedRealization: A complete count needs a checklist that rules out every other possibility.
beats.transitionIn: Look back at the same four paths.
beats.prompt: Does seeing four working paths prove that there is no fifth path?

visual.ariaLabel: The same four movement sequences found in the opening puzzle

options.text: Yes. Four paths look like enough.
No. We need a way to rule out every other path.

feedback.yes-four-look-complete: A list can look finished and still stop too soon.
feedback.no-need-checklist: Right. We need to know where every possible path would have to appear.

beats.correctFeedback: Right. A list of examples is not yet a complete count.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Think about whether a path we have not imagined could still exist.

steps.body: To be certain, we need a checklist that covers every possible number of moves—not just the paths already on the screen.

resolution.takeaway: First organize the paths. Then finish every part of the checklist.

beats.purpose: Organize the paths already found without pretending that this alone proves completeness.
beats.expectedRealization: Number of moves gives every found path one clear place.
beats.transitionIn: Start with the paths we already have. Sort them by how many moves they use.
beats.prompt: Put each path into the right group.
beats.correctFeedback: Good. Every path we found now has one clear place.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Count the moves in each path and try again.

resolution.takeaway: We organized what we found. We have not yet proved that each group is finished—or that these are the only possible groups.

beats.purpose: Use the groups as a complete checklist and exhaust every possible move count.
beats.expectedRealization: The groups prove completeness only when every group is finished and longer paths are ruled out.
beats.transitionIn: Now use each group as a checklist. Finish the small count inside every row.
beats.prompt: Match each finished list to its number of moves.

items.text: No paths: four smallest moves already total 4

beats.correctFeedback: Yes. Now every possible number of moves has been checked.
beats.incorrectFeedback: For each row, ask what positive move sizes could total exactly 3.

cases.label: 4 or more moves
items: Impossible: the minimum total is already 4

visual.ariaLabel: A complete checklist of paths grouped by number of moves

steps.title: One move
steps.body: To land on 3 in one move, the move must be 3.

steps.title: Two moves
steps.body: The positive ordered pairs totaling 3 are 1 + 2 and 2 + 1.

steps.title: Three moves
steps.body: Three positive moves totaling 3 must be 1 + 1 + 1.

steps.title: Four or more moves
steps.body: Even four minimum-size moves total at least 4, so no longer path can work.

resolution.takeaway: The groups create a complete checklist. We can finish each smaller group and prove there is nowhere else a path could hide.

beats.purpose: Name the two rigor conditions in plain language first, then supply their mathematical terms.
beats.expectedRealization: The count is trustworthy because every path is included once and each smaller group is finishable.
beats.heading: Now we can trust the count
beats.body: We checked every possible number of moves, so every path is included. Mathematicians call that exhaustive. A path has only one number of moves, so nothing is counted twice. That is non-overlapping. And each smaller group was easy to finish.

beats.purpose: Name the method only after the learner has used it to complete a proof.
beats.expectedRealization: Casework is the name for the complete, non-repeating split the learner just built.
beats.transitionIn: You just turned one uncertain list into several small lists you could completely check.
beats.name: Casework
beats.conciseDefinition: Casework means splitting one hard count into smaller counts that you can finish and check.
beats.formalization: every possibility included + nothing counted twice
beats.memoryHook: Get them all. Count each once. Make the pieces easier.

beats.purpose: Shift attention from carrying out a split to choosing the feature that makes the work easier.
beats.expectedRealization: The strongest restriction often tells us what to split by.
beats.transitionOut: That worked because the last digit controlled the rule.
beats.prompt: Using 1, 2, 3, and 4 without repetition, how should we split the count of three-digit even numbers?

options.text: Look at the last digit: 2 or 4

feedback.hundreds: The first digit does not decide whether the number is even.
feedback.tens: The middle digit does not decide whether the number is even.
feedback.ones: Exactly. Every even number here ends in 2 or 4.
feedback.size: That split covers the numbers, but it does not make the even-number rule easier.

beats.correctFeedback: Right—the even-number rule tells us to split by the last digit.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Which digit decides whether the whole number is even?

visual.ariaLabel: Two digit patterns ending in 2 or 4, with six numbers in each group

steps.title: Fix the last digit
steps.body: Once 2 or 4 is fixed at the end, there are 3 choices for the first digit and then 2 choices for the middle digit.

steps.title: Add the two groups
steps.body: Every even number ends in exactly one of those digits, so the total is 6 + 6 = 12.

resolution.takeaway: Fixing the digit that controls the rule turns one count into two easy counts.

beats.purpose: Apply the same position-based split to the approved authentic problem without duplicating it first.
beats.expectedRealization: Exactly one zero gives every valid number one legal zero position and two simple counts.
beats.transitionIn: Same strategy, new restriction: exactly one digit is 0.
beats.transitionOut: That worked because exactly one zero gave every number one place to go.
beats.whyNow: Exactly one zero in a three-digit number splits naturally by the zero's position, making the case partition concrete and checkable.
beats.entryBridge: Where can the zero go? Start there.
beats.exitBridge: Exactly one zero made two clean groups: zero in the tens place or zero in the ones place.
beats.reusedRepresentation: Outcome cards that physically sort into labeled, non-overlapping bins.
learnerPrompts: Once its place is fixed, how many choices remain?
Did the two groups count every number exactly once?
beats.correctFeedback: Right: 162. Now watch the two groups account for every number.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Keep your count. Let's build the two groups and check it.

steps.title: Choose where the zero goes
steps.body: It cannot be the first digit of a three-digit number, so it must be in the tens place or the ones place.

steps.title: Finish each group
steps.body: In either pattern, the two other digits each have 9 choices from 1 through 9.

steps.title: Put the groups together
steps.body: A number with exactly one zero cannot be in both groups, so 81 + 81 counts every number once.

resolution.takeaway: The zero's position gave us two groups we could finish and check.

beats.purpose: Keep attention on why the split worked rather than on the contest answer alone.
beats.expectedRealization: The condition gave every outcome one place and simplified the remaining choices.
beats.heading: Why that split worked
beats.body: Exactly one zero gave each number one place to go: zero in the tens place or zero in the ones place. We could finish both smaller counts and add them.
beats.transitionOut: Try the same three checks on your own: get them all, count each once, and make the pieces easier.

beats.purpose: Begin independent evidence with a reusable student-facing question sequence.
beats.heading: Your turn
beats.body: Before calculating, ask: What should I split by? Will every answer land in one group? Does the split make each group easier?

beats.purpose: Check a direct transfer in which parity supplies two clean groups.
beats.expectedRealization: Even sums split into odd-plus-odd and even-plus-even.
beats.whyNow: This checks whether the learner can construct complete groups from a familiar condition.
beats.entryBridge: What should we split by? Let the even-sum rule guide you.
beats.exitBridge: The sum rule gave two clean groups: odd + odd and even + even.
learnerPrompts: Which kinds of digit pairs make an even sum?
beats.incorrectFeedback: Check every way two digits can have an even sum.

visual.ariaLabel: Odd plus odd and even plus even groups, four codes each

steps.body: An even sum comes from two odd digits or two even digits. Each group has 2 choices for each position.

resolution.takeaway: 2 × 2 + 2 × 2 = 8, and every code belongs to exactly one of the two groups.

beats.purpose: Check systematic completion when the group sizes decrease.
beats.expectedRealization: Fixing the left card turns the remaining choices into a short row-by-row count.
beats.whyNow: Unequal group sizes require the learner to finish each group rather than repeat one multiplication.
beats.entryBridge: Try the same idea here. What could you fix first?
beats.exitBridge: Fixing the left card made five short rows with sizes 4, 3, 2, 1, and 0.
learnerPrompts: If the left card is fixed, which larger cards can go on the right?
beats.incorrectFeedback: Fix one left card at a time and count the larger choices on the right.

visual.ariaLabel: Table of larger right-card choices for each fixed left card

steps.body: Every arrangement has one left card, so the rows cannot overlap. Adding the row counts gives 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 + 0.

resolution.takeaway: Fix one part, finish that row, and keep going until no row is left.

beats.purpose: Mix casework with a constrained distribution representation.
beats.expectedRealization: Fixing Box A makes the remaining positive split short enough to list.
beats.whyNow: This changes the setting while preserving the need to choose and finish complete groups.
beats.entryBridge: What should you split by to make the remaining list short?
beats.exitBridge: Once Box A was fixed, the remaining counters had only a few possible splits.
learnerPrompts: How many counters can Box A contain while B and C stay nonempty?
beats.incorrectFeedback: Try fixing the number in Box A first.

visual.ariaLabel: Counter distributions grouped by the number in Box A

steps.body: Box A can contain 1, 2, or 3 counters. Those groups contain 3, 2, and 1 distributions.

resolution.takeaway: 3 + 2 + 1 = 6. Fixing A made every smaller list easy to finish.

beats.purpose: Test whether the learner can choose the rare large token as the clean split.
beats.expectedRealization: The number of 5-point tokens creates two complete, manageable groups.
beats.whyNow: The learner must choose a useful split rather than manage duplicate orientations or invoke a future technique.
beats.entryBridge: This time, one token size gives an especially short split. Which one?
beats.exitBridge: Splitting by the number of 5-point tokens left only two groups to finish.
learnerPrompts: How many 5-point tokens could a score of 6 contain?
beats.incorrectFeedback: Split into one 5-point token or no 5-point tokens, then finish each list.

visual.ariaLabel: Score-token collections grouped by whether they contain a 5-point token

steps.body: A score of 6 can use at most one 5-point token. With one, the rest is forced. With none, use zero, one, two, or three 2-point tokens.

resolution.takeaway: The two groups contain 1 + 4 = 5 collections, with nowhere else for a collection to go.

beats.purpose: Check authentic transfer where the final digit is the useful split among several restrictions.
beats.expectedRealization: The multiple-of-5 rule creates the complete final-digit groups 0 and 5.
beats.whyNow: The problem disguises casework among several digit restrictions and requires an independent choice of split.
beats.entryBridge: Try the same idea here: which restriction gives the cleanest split?
beats.exitBridge: The multiple-of-5 rule gave exactly two final-digit groups: 0 and 5.
learnerPrompts: What can the last digit be?
How many numbers end in 5? How many end in 0?
Did those two groups count every valid number exactly once?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct—there are 84 numbers. Now check the two groups.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Start with the multiple-of-5 rule: what can the last digit be?

steps.title: End in 5
steps.body: The first digit has 4 choices, followed by 4 and then 3 choices.

steps.title: End in 0
steps.body: The digit 5 must fill one of the first three places, then the other two places have 4 and 3 choices.

resolution.takeaway: Every multiple of 5 ends in 0 or 5, never both. So 48 + 36 = 84.

beats.purpose: Consolidate the three practical tests before creating the next lesson's tension.
beats.expectedRealization: A useful split gets every possibility once and makes the pieces easier.
beats.transitionIn: Before we change the zero problem, keep the three checks you used all lesson.
beats.prompt: Which questions tell you that a split is useful? Select all three.

options.text: Did the smaller pieces become easier?
Are all the groups the same size?

beats.correctFeedback: Exactly. Those are the three checks.
beats.incorrectFeedback: A useful split does not need equal-sized groups. Focus on coverage, repeats, and easier pieces.

visual.ariaLabel: Three-part checklist for a useful case split

resolution.takeaway: A useful case split covers every possibility, counts nothing twice, and makes the smaller pieces easier to finish.

beats.purpose: Create the overlap tension for the next lesson without naming or teaching its method.
beats.expectedRealization: The obvious position groups become messy when the condition changes from exactly one zero to at least one zero.
beats.transitionIn: Remember the problem with exactly one zero? Now change just one thing.
beats.prompt: If the condition becomes at least one zero, do 'zero in tens' and 'zero in ones' still count every number just once?
beats.takeaway: No. The number 100 belongs in both obvious groups. We could repair the overlap, but the counting is getting messy. There may be a cleaner way to count—let's leave that question open.

notes: Final human-reviewed gold-benchmark revision; no automated lesson generation was used.
The opening now separates sorting found outcomes from proving the list complete.
Worked resolutions pair each substantial question with its own visual or controlled animation.
